title: Focus Groups: How to Plan, Recruit & Run Them (2026 Guide)
summary: A focus group brings a small group together to discuss a product or service. Our 2026 guide covers how to plan, run, and analyze focus groups that produce real insight.

Launching a product without hearing from the people who will use it is guesswork. Focus groups help close that gap by bringing together a small group of real users, either in person or online, to discuss their experiences, opinions, and reactions.


When they’re done well, focus groups uncover the *why* behind user behavior in ways surveys can’t. When they’re done poorly, they produce polished transcripts filled with what participants think they should say instead of what they actually believe.


This guide covers both sides: what focus groups are, when to use them, where they fall short, how to run them successfully, and how to turn discussions into insights your team can actually use.


**TL;DR:** A focus group is a moderated group discussion with a small group of people used to explore opinions, reactions, and motivations around a product, service, or concept. They’re best for exploring ideas early in the research process and understanding user perspectives. They’re less effective for measuring real behavior or reaching statistical confidence.


To run an effective focus group:


-


Set a clear objective


-


Recruit and screen the right participants


-


Write an open-ended discussion guide


-


Moderate without leading


-


Record with consent


-


Analyze the transcript for themes or patterns

## What is a focus group?


A focus group is a[qualitative research method](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/ux-research-methods-guide) where a small, selected group of people discusses a product, service, or concept while a moderator guides the conversation. The goal is to understand participants’ opinions, reactions, and decision-making processes through the conversation.


Unlike surveys or one-on-one interviews, focus groups encourage participants to respond to each other’s ideas. Those interactions often reveal shared language, unexpected concerns, and new perspectives that researchers may not uncover through individual feedback alone.


Organizations often use focus groups to:


-


Explore customer needs


-


Test new product concepts


-


Evaluate messaging


-


Gather feedback on prototypes


-


Better understand user experiences

## Types of focus groups


Not every focus group follows the same format. The right approach depends on your research goals, participants, budget, and how much structure the discussion requires.


### Single-moderator group


The standard setup: one moderator, 6 to 10 participants, one discussion guide. Good default for most UX and product questions.


### Dual-moderator group


Two moderators split the work, one keeping the discussion flowing and the other making sure every question gets covered. Useful for dense topics where a solo moderator would drop threads.


### Dueling-moderator group


Two moderators deliberately take opposing positions to draw out debate. Handy when you want to pressure-test how strongly people hold an opinion.


### Two-way group


One group watches another group discuss a topic, then reacts to what they heard. This works when you want a second layer of interpretation, for example experts responding to customers.


### Mini focus group


Four or five participants instead of the usual six to ten. Smaller groups go deeper on sensitive or complex subjects and give quieter people more room.


### Online groups, synchronous and asynchronous


Synchronous groups happen live over video. Asynchronous groups run over hours or days in a shared thread, so participants respond on their own time. Asynchronous formats reach busy or dispersed audiences but lose the real-time spark of a live room.


## Why focus groups are worth running


Focus groups remain a valuable research method because they help teams understand the reasons behind customer opinions, behaviors, and decision making. While they won’t replace quantitative research, they can uncover insights that surveys and analytics often miss.


### Depth of insight


Focus groups help researchers understand the reasoning behind customer decisions, not just the decisions themselves. Participants explain both the practical and emotional factors influencing their choices, giving teams valuable context that quantitative data alone can’t provide.


### Real-time reactions


Watching participants respond to a product, concept, or prototype in real time helps researchers identify moments of confusion, excitement, or hesitation. Moderators can ask follow-up questions immediately, uncovering insights that would likely be missed in a survey.


### Opportunities to probe


One of the biggest advantages of a moderated discussion is the ability to explore unexpected responses. When participants raise an interesting point, moderators can ask follow-up questions to better understand the reasoning behind their feedback.


### Idea generation


Participants often build on each other’s comments, leading to new ideas and perspectives that may not emerge during individual interviews. This collaborative discussion makes focus groups especially useful during concept development and early-stage product research.


### Efficiency


A single focus group allows researchers to gather qualitative feedback from multiple participants at once. For teams working with limited time or resources, this can provide valuable early insights before investing in more extensive research.


## Limitations of focus groups


Like any research method, focus groups have limitations. Understanding these drawbacks helps researchers choose the right method for their goals and avoid drawing conclusions that the data can’t support.


### The say-do gap


Focus groups capture what participants say they would do, which doesn’t always match what they do in practice. Memory, social pressure, and the desire to give thoughtful answers can all influence responses. If your goal is to understand actual behavior, methods like usability testing, analytics, or observational research are often a better fit.


### Moderator influence


Even experienced moderators can unintentionally influence a discussion through their wording, tone, or reactions. Small cues, such as agreeing too enthusiastically with one participant, can shape the direction of the conversation and discourage alternative viewpoints.


### Group think


Participants may hesitate to disagree with the group or change their opinions as the discussion unfolds. This tendency toward[group think](https://www.verywellmind.com/what-is-groupthink-2795213) can limit honest feedback and make certain perspectives appear more widely shared than they actually are.


### Small samples


Focus groups typically include only a small number of participants, so their findings shouldn’t be treated as statistically representative of a larger audience. They’re best used to explore ideas and identify patterns, not measure prevalence.


### Privacy limits


Some participants may be uncomfortable discussing sensitive or personal experiences in a group setting. For topics involving health, finances, workplace issues, or other private matters,[one-on-one interviews](https://www.greatquestion.com/features/interviews) often produce more candid feedback.


## When to use focus groups


Focus groups work best when you need to explore how people think, react, and make decisions. They are especially useful early in the research process, when you are still shaping ideas and identifying questions to investigate further.


### Concept development


Focus groups help teams compare early product ideas before investing in development. Participants can react to multiple concepts, explain their preferences, and raise concerns that may not surface during internal planning.


### Usability feedback


A group discussion can reveal common points of friction in a prototype or product experience. It can also show how different users approach the same task, helping teams identify areas that need clearer design or instructions.


### Feature evaluation


Before building a new feature, focus groups can help you understand whether it fits users’ existing workflows and how it compares with the tools they already use. This early feedback can help teams avoid investing in features that do not solve a meaningful problem.


### Experience mapping


Focus groups can bring together different perspectives on a[customer or product journey](https://miro.com/templates/customer-journey-map/) . By comparing experiences, participants can help identify the moments that create confusion, frustration, or satisfaction.


## When a focus group is not the right method


Focus groups are not suitable for every research question. Consider another method when:


-


**You need to measure behavior, not opinion** . Use analytics, observational research, or unmoderated usability testing to see what people do rather than asking them to predict or describe their behavior.


-


**The topic is sensitive or personal** .[One-on-one interviews](https://www.greatquestion.com/features/interviews) give participants more privacy and may lead to more candid responses.


-


**You need feedback from a large audience** . A focus group usually includes no more than 10 participants. Surveys or other scalable methods are better suited to broader research.


When you need the depth of a moderated conversation across dozens or hundreds of participants, Great Question’s AI Moderation may offer another option. It conducts one-on-one, moderated-style interviews at scale and groups responses into themes.


AI-moderated research can complement focus groups rather than replace them. For example, you might use a small live group to explore a topic and refine your questions, then run a larger AI-moderated study to determine how consistently those themes appear across a broader audience.


## Focus groups for UX research vs. market research


Focus groups are used in both UX research and market research, but the goals differ.


In UX research, focus groups explore how people interact with a product, including its usability, functionality, and overall experience. The findings help teams improve how the product works and how users engage with it.


In market research, focus groups examine broader topics such as brand perception, purchasing decisions, customer preferences, and market trends. The findings are typically used to guide positioning, messaging, and go-to-market strategy.


The method is similar in both settings, but the research questions and definitions of success are different.


## How to run a focus group, step by step


A successful focus group depends on careful planning. Follow these steps to recruit the right participants, guide a productive discussion, and turn the findings into useful recommendations.


1. **Define your research objective.** Start with a single, specific question you want the focus group to answer. A clear objective helps guide participant recruitment, discussion questions, and analysis.
2. **Choose your participants (6 to 10 per group).** Recruit six to 10 people who reflect your target audience. Smaller groups may not provide enough range, while larger groups can be difficult to manage. Consider recruiting 20% to 30% more participants than you need to account for last-minute cancellations.
3. **Pick a skilled moderator.** The moderator should keep the discussion moving, encourage quieter participants, and manage dominant voices without taking sides. Strong moderation helps ensure the conversation remains balanced and focused.
4. **Write a discussion guide with open-ended questions.** Treat the discussion guide as a roadmap rather than a script. Use open-ended prompts such as “Walk me through how you…” instead of questions that can be answered with yes or no. Start with broad questions, then move into more specific topics. Leave time for follow-up questions when participants raise unexpected or useful points.
5. **Recruit and screen participants.** Use a[screener survey](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/screener-survey-guide) to filter candidates against your criteria before you commit. Tools like Great Question handle[recruitment](https://www.greatquestion.com/features/research-recruitment) , screening, scheduling, and incentives in one workflow. Confirm participation 24 to 48 hours ahead to cut no-shows.
6. **Set up the session.** For in-person groups, choose a neutral, distraction-free room where participants can see one another. For remote groups, use a reliable video platform, test the technology in advance, and provide clear instructions for joining. Collect recording consent before the discussion begins.
7. **Guide without leading.** Begin by explaining the purpose of the session and setting basic ground rules, such as allowing one person to speak at a time and welcoming different viewpoints. Start with broad questions, then narrow the discussion. Use neutral follow-ups such as “Can you tell me more?” Avoid praising or agreeing with specific responses, which can influence the group. Make space for quieter participants and redirect anyone who begins to dominate the conversation.
8. **Record and take notes.** With participants’ consent, record the discussion and assign a dedicated note-taker. Notes can capture body language, hesitation, and group dynamics that may not be obvious from the transcript alone. Store the recording securely and back it up after the session.
9. **Analyze themes and synthesize findings.** Transcribe the discussion and review it several times. Tag recurring themes, emotions, pain points, and areas of disagreement. Look for patterns across participants, but do not ignore conflicting views. Differences in perspective often reveal important audience segments or unmet needs.
10. **Share insights with stakeholders.** Summarize the research in a concise report that includes the main themes, supporting quotes, and clear recommendations. Explain what each finding means for the product, strategy, or next research step. A focused one-page summary is often more useful than a lengthy transcript that leaves stakeholders to interpret the findings themselves.

## Focus group exercises and activities


A focus group does not have to rely on questions alone. Structured activities can help participants express reactions, priorities, and mental models that may not emerge through direct discussion.


-


**Word association:** Show participants a brand, product, concept, or screen and ask them to share the first words that come to mind. This quick exercise helps surface immediate impressions and emotional reactions.


-


**Card sorting:** Give participants cards representing features, topics, or content and ask them to group or rank them. Card sorting can reveal how users organize information and which elements they consider most important.


-


**Ranking and prioritization:** Ask the group to rank several options from most to least useful, important, or appealing. The discussion behind the rankings often provides more insight than the final order itself.


-


**Drawing or sketching:** Invite participants to sketch how they picture a process, experience, or ideal solution. The drawings do not need to be polished. Even simple sketches can reveal assumptions and mental models that are difficult to explain in words.


-


**Role-play:** Ask participants to act out a realistic scenario, such as returning a product or contacting customer support. Role-play helps researchers observe friction points as they happen rather than relying only on participants’ descriptions.


## How many people should be in a focus group?


A standard focus group usually includes 6 to 10 participants. Fewer than six may limit the range of perspectives, while groups larger than 10 can be difficult to manage and may give dominant participants too much influence.


For sensitive, technical, or complex topics, a mini focus group of four or five participants may work better. Smaller groups give each person more time to speak and can support more detailed discussion.


Group size is separate from the number of sessions you run. For one audience segment, plan to conduct three to six groups so you can identify recurring themes. You have likely reached saturation when additional groups stop producing meaningful new insights.


## How much do focus groups pay in incentives?


Focus group incentives vary based on session length, topic complexity, participant criteria, and location. Standard consumer focus groups often pay between $50 and $125 per session. Studies that require[specialized](https://focusinsite.com/incentivizing-recruits-focus-groups-show-money/) medical, technical, or senior-level business experience may offer $150 to $500 or more.


Incentives do not have to be paid in cash. Gift cards, products, vouchers, and subscriptions may also be appropriate. The amount and format should reflect the time, expertise, and effort you are asking participants to contribute.


## Online vs. in-person vs. hybrid


The right format depends on your research goals, budget, participant availability, and whether the study requires physical interaction with a product.


**Online focus groups** run over video tools like Zoom or Google Meet. They are more convenient, cheaper, and easier to schedule, and they are ideal when your audience is spread out or the topic does not need physical product interaction.


**In-person focus groups** put everyone in one room. This traditional format gives you richer non-verbal cues, body language, and facial expressions, and it suits topics that need people to handle a physical product.


**Hybrid focus groups** , where some join in the room and others dial in, need extra care. Remote participants go quiet while in-room voices dominate, so assign a co-moderator to watch the video feed and actively bring remote people in. Keep the in-room group to four or fewer to hold the balance.


### Setting up a remote focus group


Choose a reliable video platform with screen sharing, gallery view, and breakout room capabilities. These features make it easier to present prototypes, keep participants visible, and run smaller group activities.


Great Question’s scheduling tools allow participants to choose a session time through a booking link and receive automated email and SMS reminders. After the session, the recording can be added to the research repository for team review and AI-assisted analysis.


### Recording consent for remote sessions


Always obtain participants’ consent before recording a remote focus group. You can collect consent through the screener, the registration process, or a confirmation prompt when participants join.


Recording laws vary by location. If participants are joining from different states or countries, confirm the applicable requirements before the session. California, Florida, and Pennsylvania are among the states that generally require all parties to consent to a recording.


A written confirmation before the session, followed by verbal confirmation at the start, provides a clear record of consent.


## How to analyze focus group data


Start by organizing the material you collected.[Transcribe the recording](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/how-to-transcribe-an-interview) , then review the transcript several times to become familiar with the discussion and identify early patterns.


Next, code the transcript by tagging comments with themes or concepts. Look at how often each theme appears, how strongly participants respond, and where opinions differ. Then group related codes into broader findings and support each one with direct quotes from the session.


AI can speed up this first stage of analysis, but human review still matters. Great Question can group similar comments into themes and link each theme to the exact point in the transcript where it appeared, allowing researchers to verify the evidence behind the summary.


Automated clustering can help teams work through large volumes of transcripts, while researchers provide the context and judgment needed to decide which findings matter.


Finally, compare the findings with your original research objective. Ask whether the results confirm your assumptions, challenge them, or introduce new questions. The goal of analysis is to support a decision, not simply summarize the discussion.


## Common focus group use cases and example questions


Focus group questions should be open-ended and tied to a clear research objective. The following examples can be adapted for common UX research use cases.


### First impressions


Use case: gauging reactions to a new app design or website layout.


-


What are your first thoughts when you see this interface?


-


What stands out about the layout and the design elements here?


-


Is there anything unclear or unexpected?


### Understanding user needs


Use case: identifying the features users want from a new tool.


-


What features do you find most valuable in the tools you use now?


-


What tasks do you wish were easier to accomplish?


-


What is missing from your current experience?


### Testing usability


Use case: checking how users interact with a prototype.


-


How easy was it to complete the task with this prototype?


-


Were there points where you felt confused about what to do next?


-


What would have made the experience easier?


Related read


[The complete guide to prototype testing](https://www.greatquestion.com/ux-research/prototype-testing-guide)


### Understanding pain points


Use case: understanding frustrations with a current or legacy product.


-


Describe a recent time when your current product did not meet your needs.


-


What are the biggest challenges you run into with the app?


-


How do you currently work around these problems?


### Feature prioritization


Use case: deciding what to build first.


-


Of the features we discussed, which should come first, and why?


-


Which would have the most positive impact on your daily use?


-


Which option would you be least likely to use?


## Best practices for running focus groups


Following a consistent set of best practices can help reduce bias, improve participation, and produce more useful findings.


-


Define exactly what the session should answer before recruiting participants.


-


Recruit people who reflect your target audience and represent a range of perspectives.


-


Use an experienced moderator who can manage group dynamics without influencing responses.


-


Create a comfortable environment so participants speak openly, online or in person.


-


Protect participant information and follow appropriate research and privacy standards.


-


Start and end on time to respect participants’ schedules.


-


Give every participant an opportunity to contribute.


-


Look for patterns across the discussion without overlooking conflicting viewpoints.


-


Offer an incentive that reflects the time, expertise, and effort required.

### Respondent


[Respondent](https://www.respondent.io/recruit-participants) is a recruiting marketplace for finding verified consumers and professionals, with filters by job title, industry, and skill. It is a solid participant source. It is not where you run or analyze the session, though, so you still need separate tools for hosting and synthesis, and the participants are a paid panel rather than your own customers.


### Discuss.io


[Discuss.io](https://www.discuss.io/) supports online focus groups and provides access to a global participant network. It can be a good fit for market research teams that need to reach new audiences across different regions. Because it uses its own participant panel and research workflow, it may function more as a standalone solution than as part of an existing research repository.


### Collabito


[Collabito](https://www.collabito.com/video-focus-groups/) is a browser-based platform for video focus groups, with automatic recording and no software install for participants. It handles the live session well. It is focused on facilitation, so recruitment, screening, and deeper analysis live elsewhere.


### FocusGroupIt


[FocusGroupIt](https://www.focusgroupit.com/) supports asynchronous, text-based focus groups that participants can join through a shared link. Discussions can remain open for several days or weeks, giving participants flexibility to respond on their own schedules. This format works well for extended asynchronous research, but it does not provide the live interaction of a moderated video session or broader synthesis across a research program.


## The bottom line


Focus groups help teams understand the language, reasoning, and emotions behind user opinions. Their value depends on clear research goals, carefully selected participants, skilled moderation, and analysis that connects the discussion to a practical decision.


They are most useful as one part of a broader research plan. Use focus groups to explore ideas and understand perspectives, then combine them with interviews, usability testing, analytics, or other behavioral methods when you need to understand what users actually do.


AI can support the first stage of analysis by organizing transcripts and identifying recurring themes. Researchers still need to verify the evidence, interpret the context, and decide what the findings mean for the product.

## Frequently asked questions


What is a focus group?


A focus group is a moderated discussion where a small group of selected people, usually 6 to 10, talks through their opinions and reactions to a product, service, or concept while a moderator guides the conversation.


How many people should be in a focus group?


A standard focus group includes six to 10 participants. For sensitive or complex topics, a mini group of four or five participants often works better. Plan to run three to six groups per audience to confirm recurring themes.


Do you get paid to take part in a focus group?


Usually, yes. Participants are typically offered $50 to $125 for a standard consumer focus group, while specialized studies may offer $150 to $500 or more. Incentives can include cash, gift cards, products, or other rewards.


Are online focus groups as good as in-person?


It depends on your research goals. Online focus groups are more convenient and cost-effective for most studies, while in-person sessions provide richer nonverbal cues and work better when participants need to interact with a physical product. Hybrid sessions can also be effective but typically require a co-moderator to keep remote participants engaged.


What is the difference between a focus group and a user interview?


A focus group is a moderated discussion where participants react to each other’s ideas and experiences. A user interview is a one-on-one conversation that allows for deeper exploration of individual perspectives and is often better suited to sensitive topics. Many research teams use both methods together.
